name: Hip Osteoarthritis
summary: Hip OA commonly causes groin/anterior thigh pain, mobility loss and reduced walking function; rehabilitation emphasizes exercise, education and selected manual therapy.

looksLike: Difficulty shoes/socks, stairs or rising from low chair
selfCare: Use assistive device temporarily if it improves safety and walking quality

assess: Hip ROM, especially flexion and rotation
Functional tasks such as stairs and sit-to-stand

tests.name: Hip ROM Pattern
tests.purpose: Identify mobility deficits typical of hip OA.
tests.positive: Painful restriction, often particularly internal rotation and flexion.

tests.name: FABER
tests.purpose: Assess hip mobility and symptom provocation.
tests.positive: Groin pain or marked restriction supports hip involvement.

stages.label: Education, Mobility & Baseline Strength
stages.goal: Reduce disability and build confidence in movement.

stages.label: Progressive Lower-Limb Capacity
stages.goal: Improve strength, balance and walking/stair function.

stages.label: Long-Term Management / Escalation
stages.goal: Maintain independence; identify when joint-replacement opinion is appropriate.
do: Medical/orthopaedic review for persistent major quality-of-life limitation
dose: Maintain strength and aerobic program long term
moveOn: Independent self-management or escalation when appropriate

returnCriteria: Focus on patient-specific walking, stair, work and recreation goals.
Referral for arthroplasty opinion when quality of life is substantially affected despite appropriate nonsurgical management.

logic: Prioritize walking tolerance, hip strength and functional independence.
Manual traction/mobilization is useful only if it improves movement enough to support active work.
Differentiate hip OA from lumbar referral and other hip pathology.
structures: Periarticular muscles and functional kinetic chain
mechanism: Multifactorial age, morphology, previous injury, load and metabolic factors
classification: Radiographic OA when imaging is indicated
investigations: Typical OA may be diagnosed clinically; imaging is used for atypical features or when it changes management.
Radiographs are common when surgical planning or diagnostic clarification is needed.
manual: Hip joint mobilization and soft-tissue techniques may be used for selected pain/mobility deficits alongside exercise.
Manual therapy should not be the sole treatment.
Posterior/anterior/lateral glides selected by impairment and response
Soft-tissue techniques for surrounding muscle discomfort
Hip long-axis traction: gentle test force first, then sustained/intermittent bouts if pain reduces.
Posterior/anterior/lateral glides: select from movement restriction and response.
Avoid aggressive mobilization in severe osteoporosis or irritable inflammatory states.
modalities: Do not build OA care around electrotherapy.
Exercise, education and self-management remain central.
Heat can be used 10–15 minutes for comfort before exercise.
TENS may be trialed but is optional.
dosing: Bridge or hip extension: 2–3 sets × 8–15 reps.
progression: Increase resistance, walking volume and functional depth
Add unilateral balance and step tasks when safe
Progress external resistance, walking distance and step height.
Use an assistive device temporarily if it improves gait safety and allows more activity.
Refer for orthopedic discussion when disability remains severe despite adequate conservative care.
mistakes: Avoiding strengthening because the joint is arthritic
Treating only stiffness with passive techniques
Delaying appropriate referral when disability remains severe
Waiting for zero pain before progressing function.
pearls: Groin pain plus loss of hip internal rotation is a common clinical pattern.
2025 hip OA CPG supports exercise and manual therapy as components of rehabilitation.
education: Explain the role of regular movement and strength.
Teach pacing for longer walking days.
Discuss assistive devices as tools for activity, not signs of failure.
escalation: Orthopedic review when pain and disability remain severe despite adequate conservative management

tests.name: Hip ROM Pattern
tests.purpose: Identify mobility deficits typical of hip OA.
tests.positive: Painful restriction, often particularly internal rotation and flexion.
procedure: Assess internal and external rotation with pelvis stabilized.
tests.interpretation: Supports hip OA in the appropriate clinical context; not diagnostic alone.

tests.name: FABER
tests.purpose: Assess hip mobility and symptom provocation.
tests.positive: Groin pain or marked restriction supports hip involvement.
tests.handPlacement: Stabilize opposite pelvis; gently guide tested knee.
procedure: Flex, abduct and externally rotate tested hip.
Note groin vs posterior pain and range.
tests.interpretation: Useful supportive finding with history and ROM pattern.

story.headline: The sock test: when a morning routine tells you about the hip
story.scene: A 66-year-old man stops halfway through putting on a sock. 'My groin aches, turning my foot inward feels stuck, and my shoes are winning this argument.' His back has been blamed for months.
story.dialogue: Patient: 'Isn't groin pain always from a muscle pull?' Therapist: 'The hip joint would like a chance to explain itself.'
story.clue: Groin or anterior thigh pain with restricted hip internal rotation and functional limits can suggest hip OA, though hip, spine and other conditions can overlap.
story.twist: Hip discomfort can be felt at the knee, and the back can mimic hip symptoms. Serious causes such as fracture, septic joint or avascular necrosis need screening.
story.aha: Sometimes the most useful assessment starts with 'Show me how you put on your socks.'
story.patientTranslation: Joint changes in the hip may make bending, turning and walking harder. We can often improve function through tailored exercises and practical changes, even when stiffness does not disappear completely.
story.clinicianReasoning: Differentiate OA from lumbar referral, nonarthritic hip pain, fracture and inflammatory causes. Assess internal rotation, function, irritability and strength. Progress hip and lower-limb strengthening and relevant walking tasks.
story.rehabBridge: Make daily movement comfortable → build hip strength and walking tolerance → restore confidence with shoes, stairs and community activities.
story.question: Groin pain, reduced hip internal rotation and difficulty putting on socks most strongly support which next step?
options: Ignore the hip and treat only the lumbar spine
Assess hip OA alongside important differentials and red flags
story.explanation: That pattern warrants a focused hip examination for OA while evaluating spinal referral and other serious or alternative causes.
